item.research_question: What is the affinity of high-entropy alloys to hydrogen and their resistance to hydrogen corrosion under high pressure?
item.material_system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), including Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) and platinum group (PGM) alloys (e.g., fcc-Ir0.231(2)Os0.090(1)Pt0.273(1)Rh0.302(2)Ru0.104(2) and hcp-Ir0.19(1)Os0.22(1)Re0.21(1)Rh0.20(1)Ru0.19(1))
item.processing_route: Powder X-ray diffraction experiments using diamond anvil cells, with pressures up to 50 GPa and ambient temperature
item.test_conditions: High pressure (up to 50 GPa) and ambient temperature, using diamond anvil cells with Ne and H2 pressure-transmitting media
key_findings: HEAs show exceptional resistance to hydride formation under high pressure
Cantor alloy and PGM alloys exhibit low hydrogen affinity despite large atomic radii of constituent atoms
Compression-induced formation of previously unknown high-entropy hydrides with PGM HEA systems as precursors
HEAs have potential applications in hydrogen economy, including hydrogen production, storage, transportation, and infrastructure
Cantor alloy is resilient in comparison to 316 Steel and Cu-Be alloy
Formation of new high-entropy hydrides in previously unexplored systems
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the affinity of HEAs to hydrogen is controlled by their crystal chemistry, which can be efficiently tested using the combination of diamond anvil cell and X-ray diffraction techniques
item.limitations: The study only investigates a limited number of HEA compositions and does not provide a complete picture of HEAs
item.future_work: Further exploration of the vast and still unexplored space of HEA compositions and their properties, including hydrogen affinity and corrosion resistance
quotes: High‐Entropy Alloys and Their Affinity with Hydrogen: From Cantor to Platinum Group Elements Alloys

records.text: Paper card. Question: What is the affinity of high-entropy alloys to hydrogen and their resistance to hydrogen corrosion under high pressure?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), including Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) and platinum group (PGM) alloys (e.g., fcc-Ir0.231(2)Os0.090(1)Pt0.273(1)Rh0.302(2)Ru0.104(2) and hcp-Ir0.19(1)Os0.22(1)Re0.21(1)Rh0.20(1)Ru0.19(1)). Processing: Powder X-ray diffraction experiments using diamond anvil cells, with pressures up to 50 GPa and ambient temperature. Test conditions: High pressure (up to 50 GPa) and ambient temperature, using diamond anvil cells with Ne and H2 pressure-transmitting media. Findings: HEAs show exceptional resistance to hydride formation under high pressure; Cantor alloy and PGM alloys exhibit low hydrogen affinity despite large atomic radii of constituent atoms; Compression-induced formation of previously unknown high-entropy hydrides with PGM HEA systems as precursors; HEAs have potential applications in hydrogen economy, including hydrogen production, storage, transportation, and infrastructure; Cantor alloy is resilient in comparison to 316 Steel and Cu-Be alloy; Formation of new high-entropy hydrides in previously unexplored systems. Mechanism: The authors propose that the affinity of HEAs to hydrogen is controlled by their crystal chemistry, which can be efficiently tested using the combination of diamond anvil cell and X-ray diffraction techniques. Limitations: The study only investigates a limited number of HEA compositions and does not provide a complete picture of HEAs. Future work: Further exploration of the vast and still unexplored space of HEA compositions and their properties, including hydrogen affinity and corrosion resistance. Quote: "High‐Entropy Alloys and Their Affinity with Hydrogen: From Cantor to Platinum Group Elements Alloys"
